name: Abimelech (Gideon's son)
title: The Self-Proclaimed King of Shechem
summary: Abimelech was a son of Gideon (Jerubbaal), born to his concubine from Shechem. Driven by ambition for power after his father's death, he obtained seventy silver shekels from the temple of Baal-Berith and hired ruthless men to massacre his half-brothers in Ophrah. Sixty-nine of Gideon’s seventy sons were killed on a single stone—only the youngest, Jotham, survived, and from Mount Gerizim he proclaimed a prophetic parable about trees choosing a thornbush as king, a warning of mutual destruction. After being declared king at the oak tree in Shechem, Abimelech ruled for three years until God sent an evil spirit between him and the city’s inhabitants. He crushed the ensuing rebellion with ruthless brutality: Shechem was razed to the ground and sown with salt, and about a thousand people died when he set fire to the fortress temple of El-Berith. During the siege of Thebez, he was mortally wounded by a millstone thrown by a woman from a tower. To avoid shame, he ordered his armor-bearer to run him through with a sword. The story serves as a powerful warning that power rooted in violence and deceit carries within it its own downfall, and that God’s righteous judgment overtakes those who seize authority through illegitimate means.

keyEvents.title: Abimelech's seizure of power
keyEvents.description: Abimelech persuades his mother's relatives in Shechem to support him as ruler instead of Gideon's other seventy sons. He receives seventy silver shekels from the temple of Baal-Berith and hires reckless and wild men who follow him.

keyEvents.title: The Massacre at Ophrah
keyEvents.description: Abimelech had his half-brothers—sixty-nine of Gideon's seventy sons—killed on one stone in Ophrah, his father's hometown. The youngest, Jotham, escaped by hiding. Afterwards, Abimelech was proclaimed king by the oak of the pillar at Shechem.

keyEvents.title: Jotham's Fable on Mount Gerizim
keyEvents.description: Jotham stood atop Mount Gerizim and shouted a prophetic fable about trees that chose a worthless thornbush as their king. He declared that mutual destruction would befall Abimelech and the citizens of Shechem as punishment for their wicked deeds against Gideon's house.

keyEvents.title: The Rebellion in Shechem
keyEvents.description: After three years of rule, God sent a spirit of discord between Abimelech and the citizens of Shechem. They turned against him under the leadership of Gaal son of Ebed, who challenged Abimelech's right to rule.

keyEvents.title: The Destruction of Shechem
keyEvents.description: Abimelech crushed the rebellion with cunning and military force. He captured the city, killed its inhabitants, demolished Shechem, and scattered salt over it. Then he set fire to the tower of the temple of El-Berith, where about a thousand men and women had taken refuge, and all perished.

keyEvents.title: The Death of Abimelech at Thebez
keyEvents.description: During the siege of Thebez, a woman dropped an upper millstone from the tower, crushing Abimelech's skull. To avoid the shame of being killed by a woman, he ordered his armor-bearer to run him through with his sword. Thus Jotham's curse was fulfilled, and God repaid the wickedness that Abimelech had done against his father's house.

versions.summary: Abimelech was the son of the judge Gideon and a concubine from Shechem. He seized power by killing his seventy half-brothers and had himself proclaimed king over Shechem. His brutal rule ended after three years when he was killed during the siege of Thebez.
versions.title: The Self-Proclaimed King
versions.reason: [minor] The word 'medhustruinde' is a spelling error. The correct word is 'medhustruen' or 'medhustru'.; [minor] The summary could be made more informative by noting that Abimelech is not counted as a judge in Israel, and that his story serves as a warning against tyrannical abuse of power.; [major] Abimelech's mother is described in Judges 8:31 as a concubine from Shechem. Although her name is unknown, the field should include an indication of this, for example 'unknown (the concubine from Shechem)' or be referred to as null with an explanation.; [major] Gideon had seventy sons (Judg 8:30). Jotham was the youngest who survived the massacre, but the list should ideally reflect that Abimelech had many half-brothers. Listing only Jotham is incomplete, even though it can be defended that he is the most named. At minimum, it should be mentioned that there were 69 other brothers.; [minor] Jotham's fable covers verses 7–15 and verse 20, but omits verses 16–19, which are also part of Jotham's speech/curse. These verses contain important parts of Jotham's message to the citizens of Shechem.; [minor] The role 'tyrant' or 'usurper' could have been added to better reflect Abimelech's character, since he was not a legitimate king but seized power through violence and deceit.; [major] The profile completely lacks footnotes. There are rich historical, archaeological, and theological details connected with Abimelech, Shechem, and this period that should be included.

versions.summary: Abimelech was the son of the judge Gideon (Jerubbaal) and his concubine from Shechem. After his father's death, he seized power by killing his seventy half-brothers on a single stone in Ophrah, funded with silver from the temple of Baal-Berith. Only the youngest brother Jotham escaped. Abimelech had himself proclaimed king over Shechem, but his brutal and illegitimate rule lasted only three years. When the men of Shechem revolted, he completely destroyed the city. During the subsequent siege of Thebez, he was mortally wounded when a woman dropped a millstone on his head. His story serves as a warning against tyrannical abuse of power and shows how God judges unjust rulers.
versions.title: The Self-Proclaimed King of Shechem
versions.reason: [major] The lifetime 'c. 1150–1147 BC' gives only 3 years, which covers only the reign period, not the entire life. Abimelech was born at least a couple of decades earlier. A more reasonable indication should either reflect the full lifespan (e.g., c. 1170–1147 BC) or be explicitly stated as the reign period.; [major] Gideon had seventy sons (Judg 8:30). Jotham was the youngest who survived, but the list of siblings should ideally mention that there were seventy brothers in total, not just Jotham. Listing only Jotham gives the impression that he was the only brother, while the text clearly states 70 sons (of whom 69 were killed and Jotham survived).; [minor] The mother is set to zero, but the Bible identifies her as a concubine/servant woman from Shechem (Judg 8:31). Although we do not know her name, the field could be set to a descriptive value or kept as zero with a footnote.; [minor] The expression 'the concubine' should be 'concubine' (the definite form 'the concubine' is grammatically correct, but 'his concubine from Shechem' flows better). Also: 'on one stone' is a correct biblical detail. The summary is good but can be improved with somewhat clearer theological reflection that distinguishes it from the previous version.; [minor] The role 'son of Gideon' or 'half-brother' could be considered to clarify his family position, but existing roles are acceptable.; [minor] In the event 'The killing of the seventy brothers', it is said that he killed his seventy half-brothers, but the biblical text states that 69 were killed (Jotham survived). The wording should be clarified to 'his half-brothers – seventy men – on one stone' as the text actually expresses it (Judg 9:5 mentions 'seventy men'), where Jotham was the one who escaped.

versions.summary: Abimelech, son of Gideon (Jerubbaal) and his concubine from Shechem, sought to establish a kingdom through violence and deceit. After his father's death, he obtained silver from the temple of Baal-Berith in Shechem and hired ruthless men to kill his half-brothers—seventy men—on one stone at Ophrah. Only the youngest, Jotham, escaped and proclaimed from Mount Gerizim in a prophetic parable that Abimelech's rule was doomed to destruction. Appointed king over Shechem, Abimelech reigned for three years before the people turned against him. He crushed the rebellion with brutal force, completely destroyed Shechem, and set fire to the fortress temple where about a thousand people had sought refuge. During the subsequent siege of Thebez, he was mortally wounded by a millstone thrown by a woman from the city wall's tower. To avoid disgrace, he asked his armor-bearer to deliver the death blow. The story illustrates how illegitimate seizure of power and ruthless use of violence lead to self-destruction, and that God's righteous judgment strikes those who defy His order.
versions.title: The Self-Proclaimed King of Shechem
versions.reason: [minor] The reign is dated to approximately 1150–1147 BC (3 years), which aligns with Judges 9:22. The birth year of around 1170 BC is speculative but reasonable. Dating for the period of the judges is generally uncertain, but this serves as an acceptable estimate.; [major] According to Judges 9:5, Abimelech had seventy half-brothers (Gideon's sons). The list includes only Jotham, but it should also note that he had many other half-brothers. Although we do not know all the names, this should be reflected more clearly. At minimum, it should mention that Jotham was the sole survivor of 70 brothers.; [minor] The mother's name is unknown, but she is described as a concubile (pilegsh) from Shechem (Judges 8:31). The field is set to zero, which is acceptable, though a comment in the summary covers this point.; [minor] The role 'son of Gideon' or 'half-brother murderer' could be considered, but the current roles 'self-proclaimed king', 'warrior', and 'tyrant' adequately cover his main functions. Alternatively, 'ruler over Shechem' could be added for greater precision.; [minor] The footnote refers to Jotham's fable as the 'oldest known fable in the Hebrew Bible'. This is correct and widely accepted in biblical scholarship. Some scholars regard it as one of the oldest fables in world literature overall.; [minor] It states that 'seventy men' were killed, but according to Judges 9:5, 69 were killed (seventy minus Jotham). The text does indeed say 'seventy men' in a rounded form, but precision could be improved by clarifying this.

footnotes.text: The name Abimelech (אֲבִימֶלֶךְ) means 'my father is king' in Hebrew. This is ironic given that his father Gideon explicitly rejected kingship with the words, 'The Lord will rule over you' (Judg 8:23). The fact that Abimelech bore this name suggests dynastic ambitions from birth.

Archaeological excavations at Tell Balatah (ancient Shechem) have uncovered a monumental fortress temple from the Middle and Late Bronze Age with walls up to five meters thick. This corresponds to the description of the Baal-Berith/El-Berith temple in Judges 9, where about a thousand people took refuge and perished in the fire set by Abimelech.

The practice of scattering salt over a destroyed city (Judg 9:45) is known from several ancient cultures in the Near East. It symbolized curse and permanent destruction. Similar practices are documented in Assyrian and Hittite ritual texts, where salt was used as a symbol of infertility and divine judgment.

Jotham's fable (Judg 9:7–15) is considered the oldest known fable in the Hebrew Bible and one of the oldest in world literature. The olive tree, fig tree, vine, and thornbush serve as allegorical figures: the fruitful trees refuse kingship while the worthless thornbush accepts it—a sharp political satire on illegitimate leadership.

Abimelech's death at the hands of an unnamed woman became a lasting example in Israel's military tradition. In 2 Samuel 11:21, Joab refers to the incident and expects the question, 'Was it not a woman who threw a millstone down on him from the wall?'—testifying that the story was widely known as a warning.

Abimelech's three-year rule represents the first attempt at monarchy in Israel. Rabbinic tradition interprets his downfall as divine proof that legitimate kingship requires God's choice, not human violence and manipulation—a theme that anticipates the later debate surrounding the kingdoms of Saul and David.

Mount Gerizim, from which Jotham delivered his speech (Judg 9:7), was already in this period a place of sacred significance. The mountain had acoustic properties that made it possible to shout down to Shechem in the valley below. Later, the mountain became the central sanctuary for the Samaritans.
